extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and policymakers interested in political philosophy and constitutional governance (late-18th-century British public/political class)
extracted.subtask_description: A set of political-philosophical principles for preserving stable commonwealths: cautions about popular sovereignty, the role of religion and education, protection of property and church establishment, and prudent limits on reform. Geared toward guiding statesmen and public opinion about constitutional order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of perfect democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfect democracy is, therefore, the most shameless thing in the world. As it is the most shameless, it is also the most fearless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because individuals in a mass are nearer to their objects, less subject to the controlling power of fame, and confident in their own power, a large democracy risks shamelessness and lack of restraint. The people may fail to imagine they can be punished, producing impunity and moral corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular will is not the standard of right
rubrics_metrics.description: They should not be suffered to imagine that their will, any more than that of kings, is the standard of right and wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citizens must be persuaded they are no more entitled nor qualified safely to exercise arbitrary power than rulers; otherwise popular caprice will exact abject submission from officials and extinguish moral principle, judgment, and consistency of character among those who serve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid elevating occasional public approbation into moral judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Their own approbation of their own acts has to them the appearance of a public judgment in their favor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because individuals mistake local or immediate approbation for a public moral verdict, systems must guard against conflating transient popularity with legitimate moral or legal sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious and moral education as restraint on selfish will
rubrics_metrics.description: When the people have emptied themselves of all the lust of selfish will, which without religion it is utterly impossible they ever should... they will be more careful how they place power in base and incapable hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religion and moral education cultivate the internal dispositions necessary for citizens to exercise delegated power prudently; without such formation, popular nominations and exercises of power are likely to be driven by selfishness and caprice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit and virtue as criteria for public office
rubrics_metrics.description: They will confer that power... on those only in whom they may discern that predominant proportion of active virtue and wisdom, taken together and fitted to the charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appointments to authority must be made on evident virtue and wisdom rather than sordid interest, caprice, or arbitrary will; office is a grave trust, not a petty job to be distributed by fashion or favoritism.

rubrics_metrics.name: State as an intergenerational partnership
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a partnership in all science; a partnership in all art; a partnership in every virtue and in all perfection... between those who are living, those who are dead, and those who are to be born.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public institutions and laws should be treated as long-term inheritances; policies should respect obligations to past and future generations, not be altered for transient interests or fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding subversion as method of reform
rubrics_metrics.description: He should never dream of beginning its reformation by its subversion... approach to the faults of the state as to the wounds of a father, with pious awe and trembling solicitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform must be cautious and restorative rather than revolutionary and destructive; radical overthrow destroys continuity and the moral basis of society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability of jurisprudence and reverence for legal tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: The science of jurisprudence... is the collected reason of ages, combining the principles of original justice with the infinite variety of human concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not abandon longstanding legal principles and the study of jurisprudence; personal self-sufficiency and arrogance should not usurp the tribunal. Law provides stable grounds of hope and fear to guide conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of stable institutions for education and habits
rubrics_metrics.description: No certain laws... would keep the actions of men in a certain course... Nothing stable in the modes of holding property or exercising function could form a solid ground on which any parent could speculate in the education of his offspring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stable property rights, offices, and standards are prerequisites for meaningful education, habituation of honor, and the cultivation of arts and sciences; continual change breeds barbarism and dissipation of acquired cultural capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: State public finance should not jeopardize private property
rubrics_metrics.description: It is to the property of the citizen, and not to the demands of the creditor of the state, that the first and original faith of civil society is pledged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public creditor's claims cannot justifiably subsume or mortgage citizens' private property; pledges of the state should be confined to the public estate and taxation, not to confiscation of private holdings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of church establishment as essential to constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: They do not consider their church establishment as convenient, but as essential to their state... Church and state are ideas inseparable in their minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A national church establishment is presented as foundational: intertwined with education, public life, and national identity; treating it as expendable risks undermining the constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clergy independence from the treasury
rubrics_metrics.description: They certainly never have suffered, and never will suffer, the fixed estate of the church to be converted into a pension, to depend on the treasury... They tremble for their liberty, from the influence of a clergy dependent on the crown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clergy should have secure, independent provision (linked to property) rather than being state pensioners, to avoid political dependence that would harm liberty and public tranquility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church property as part of the nation's protected patrimony
rubrics_metrics.description: They have incorporated and identified the estate of the church with the mass of private property... that the provision of this establishment might be as stable as the earth on which it stands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Church revenues should be treated like private property under public guardianship and not be liable to arbitrary fiscal seizure; stability prevents politicization and preserves the institution's social functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason for public ceremonial expenditure
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the public ornament. It is the public consolation... The poorest man finds his own importance and dignity in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modest public splendor—buildings, music, decoration, dignity of persons—serves social functions: consolidating national esteem, offering consolation, and reminding the humble of shared civic dignity; such expenditure is not mere luxury but public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against confiscation and proscription as policy tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Sacrilege and proscription are not among the ways and means of our committee of supply... I HOPE WE SHALL NEVER be so totally lost... as, upon any pretext of public service, to confiscate the goods of a single unoffending citizen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The state must not resort to mass confiscation or proscription of citizens' property under political pretexts; doing so is tyrannical, cruel, and degrades victims often beyond physical punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of revolutionary legal sophistry regarding ecclesiastical persons
rubrics_metrics.description: They say that ecclesiastics are fictitious persons, creatures of the state, whom at pleasure they may destroy... that the goods they possess are not properly theirs but belong to the state which created the fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject doctrinal justifications for seizing ecclesiastical property by treating clergy as mere state creations; such sophistry enables theft and denial of ordinary moral claims of persons affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency in public faith and external obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Assembly... is engaged in a respectable deliberation how far it is bound by the treaties made with other nations under the former government... they have put the external fidelity of this virgin state on a par with its internal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A government should maintain fidelity to prior treaties and public obligations; arbitrary selection of which past acts to honor weakens external trust and internal coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of interests that favor novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The monied interest... and a new description of men had grown up... I mean the political men of letters. Men of letters, fond of distinguishing themselves, are rarely averse to innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that certain social groups (recently wealthy, intellectuals seeking distinction) are predisposed toward rapid change; their alignment can drive revolutionary agendas and should be weighed against the longer-term interests of the commonwealth.
